etymology: From the Old French abaissier, to bring low, and that from the Late Latin bassus, low — the same root as base and abate. It renders the Hebrew shaphel, to make low, and the Greek tapeinoo, to humble.
biblical_def: To abase is to bring down from a height, and Scripture makes it one of the settled operations of God’s government. The great text is Eze 21:26: “Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high.” That is not an occasional intervention but a standing policy, and it is the reason no dynasty, no reputation, and no self-estimate is secure. Nebuchadnezzar learned it in a field on all fours and confessed it afterward in the plainest words a pagan king ever spoke: “those that walk in pride he is able to abase” (Dan 4:37). Note able — the king had discovered not merely that God dislikes pride but that He possesses the power to break it, and does. Yet the word has a second and gentler use, for a man may be abased without being humiliated. Paul writes, “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Php 4:12), and treats the low estate as a lesson he had to be instructed in, no more natural to him than plenty. There is even a use in which God will not abase Himself: the LORD of hosts, like a lion over his prey, “will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them” (Isa 31:4). He humbles the proud; He is not Himself humbled by the noise of shepherds.
webster_summary: To bring down or reduce from a higher state or rank; to humble, to cast down. Applied in Scripture chiefly to God’s dealings with the proud.
webster_full: ABASE, v.t. To cast down; to reduce low; to depress; to humble; to degrade.
From the Old French abaissier; Late Latin bassus, low; allied to abate and base.
Applied to the passions, to bring down pride or arrogance.
Rendering the Hebrew shaphel, to make low (Eze 21:26; Dan 4:37).
In the passive, to be brought into a low estate, as of poverty or affliction (Php 4:12).
scriptures: Isa 31:4

For thus hath the LORD spoken unto me, Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, he will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them: so shall the LORD of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof.
Thus saith the Lord GOD; Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high.
Dan 4:37
Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.
Php 4:12
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.
corruption_summary: The age has made self-esteem a duty and lowliness a pathology, so that the very operation Scripture calls God’s mercy toward the proud is now treated as an injury to be resisted or healed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the inversion of high and low. Modern thought holds that a man’s troubles proceed chiefly from thinking too little of himself, and that the remedy is to raise his estimate of his own worth. Scripture holds the reverse: the root trouble is that man thinks too much of himself, and the remedy God most often applies is to bring him down. Eze 21:26 announces the policy in two clauses that cannot be separated — exalt him that is low and abase him that is high — and every attempt to keep the first while refusing the second collapses into a religion of self-improvement. Nebuchadnezzar is the standing case. He was not counselled into humility; he was abased into it, and he blessed God for it afterwards.

Recover the plain sense: being abased is not the failure of the Christian life but frequently its instrument. God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble, which means the low place is precisely where the supply is. Paul had to learn abasement, and he set it beside abounding as the two conditions in which a believer must be instructed — neither poverty nor plenty is safe untaught. When God brings a man down, the question is not how quickly he can be restored to his former height but what he is meant to receive at the bottom. Nebuchadnezzar came back with his reason and a doxology; that is a good exchange for a crown.
roots_summary: Late Latin bassus, low — to bring down; God’s standing policy toward the high, and a lesson the believer must learn.
roots_lines: Abase — Old French abaissier, from Late Latin bassus, low.
Kin to abate and base; the root idea is lowering, not shaming.
Hebrew shaphel, to make low (Eze 21:26).
Greek tapeinoo, to humble — the same verb used of Christ’s self-humbling (Php 2:8).
Eze 21:26 states the policy: exalt the low, abase the high.
usage: Eze 21:26 is God’s settled government, not an occasional judgment.
Dan 4:37: Nebuchadnezzar confesses God is able to abase the proud — power, not mere disapproval.
Php 4:12 shows abasement as a state to be learned, set beside abounding.

etymology: Two distinct words fell together in English. The first is from the Old French braire, to cry out, used of the ass’s harsh call. The second is from the Old French breier, to pound or crush small, used of grinding in a mortar. The Authorized Version employs both, and each carries its own lesson.
biblical_def: The first bray is the cry of a beast in want. “Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass?” (Job 6:5) — Job’s defence of his own complaining. The animal does not cry when it is fed; its noise is the honest evidence of an empty belly, and Job means that his groaning is likewise not petulance but the sound of real affliction. Scripture does not despise the cry of the sufferer, and it does not require the afflicted to pretend contentment they have not been given. The second bray is the work of the mortar, and it yields one of the bleakest verses in Proverbs: “Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him” (Pro 27:22). Grain is pounded to separate the husk from the kernel; the process works because the husk is not the grain. But pound a fool and you get a bruised fool, because his folly is not a husk clinging to him — it is his kernel. This is a doctrine of the heart, not a proverb about stubborn personalities. Affliction of itself sanctifies nobody. Pressure removes what is external; only regeneration changes what a man is. Two brayings, then: the honest cry of the hungry, and the useless pounding of the fool.
webster_summary: To utter a harsh cry, as an ass; and, from a distinct root, to pound or grind small in a mortar. Both senses stand in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: BRAY, v.i. To utter a harsh, loud cry, as an ass; hence, to make any harsh, disagreeable noise.
From the Old French braire, to cry out.
BRAY, v.t. To pound, beat, or grind small, as in a mortar with a pestle.
From the Old French breier, to break or pound; a distinct word accidentally alike in form.
Pro 27:22 employs the second sense: to bray a fool in a mortar is to pound him small.
scriptures: Job 6:5
Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder?
Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.
Job 30:7
Among the bushes they brayed; under the nettles they were gathered together.
Jer 6:29
The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire ; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away.
corruption_summary: The modern faith that hardship automatically produces character is exactly the error Pro 27:22 was written to destroy — the mortar does not convert the fool.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the doctrine of redemptive suffering without redemption. It is now a commonplace that difficulty builds people, that adversity is the universal teacher, that what does not destroy a man makes him stronger. Scripture flatly contradicts this as a general rule. Pharaoh was pounded with ten plagues and came out harder each time. Ahaz, in the time of his distress, did trespass yet more against the LORD — and the chronicler adds the terrible words this is that king Ahaz. The mortar is real, the pestle is real, and the fool comes out the other side a fool, only bruised. Suffering is not a sacrament; it does not work by the doing of the work.

Recover the plain sense: affliction is a means God uses, but it is not a mechanism that runs by itself, and its effect depends entirely on whether the Spirit attends it. The same furnace that softens wax hardens clay. Where God is pleased to sanctify a trouble, it purges dross and yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to them which are exercised thereby — note exercised, a word of active submission, not passive endurance. Where He is not, the same trouble produces only bitterness and a harder heart. So do not tell the afflicted that their pain will automatically improve them, and do not despise their crying: Job 6:5 grants the wild ass its bray.
roots_summary: Two roots, one spelling: Old French braire, to cry out, and breier, to pound small — the cry of want and the useless pounding of folly.
roots_lines: Bray (1) — Old French braire, to cry harshly, as an ass (Job 6:5).
Bray (2) — Old French breier, to pound or grind in a mortar (Pro 27:22).
The two words are unrelated in origin and fell together in English form.
The mortar separates husk from kernel — which is why it fails on a fool.
Job 6:5 defends the honesty of the sufferer’s cry.
usage: Job 6:5: the beast cries only when it lacks — the groan is evidence, not petulance.
Pro 27:22 denies that affliction of itself removes folly; the folly is the kernel, not the husk.
Distinguish the two words: one is a noise, the other a grinding.

etymology: From the Latin tentare, to try, to test, to handle — through the Old French tempter. It renders the Hebrew nasah, to prove or put to the test, and the Greek peirazo, which likewise means to test and only by consequence to solicit unto evil.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version tempt means to put to the proof, and the moral quality of the act lies wholly in who is testing whom and to what end. When God tests, it is to prove and refine: “God did tempt Abraham” (Gen 22:1) — not to discover something He did not know, but to bring out into the open a faith that could then be seen, and to set the knife and the ram in the same chapter as a picture of a Father who does not spare His Son. When Satan tests, it is to solicit and destroy, and James forbids the confusion of the two absolutely: “Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man” (Jas 1:13). But the gravest use is the third — man tempting God. That is the sin of Massah, where the people demanded a sign to settle whether the LORD was among them, and the law names it directly: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah” (Deu 6:16). Our Lord answered the devil with that very text (Mat 4:7) when invited to throw Himself from the pinnacle. To tempt God is to demand that He prove Himself on our terms, at our chosen moment, by a sign of our devising — and it is unbelief wearing the costume of faith.
webster_summary: To try; to put to the proof. Hence, according to the tempter’s design, either to prove and refine (as God does) or to entice unto evil (as Satan does).
webster_full: TEMPT, v.t. To incite or solicit to an evil act; to entice.
To try; to prove; to put to trial for the purpose of ascertaining quality.
From the Latin tentare, to handle, to try, to attempt.
To presume upon; as, to tempt God, by demanding proof of His care (Deu 6:16).
Rendering the Greek peirazo, which bears both the neutral sense of testing and the evil sense of enticing.
scriptures: Gen 22:1
And it came to pass after these things, that God did tempt Abraham, and said unto him, Abraham: and he said, Behold, here I am.
Deu 6:16
Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.
Mat 4:7
Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
Jas 1:13
Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man:
corruption_summary: The archaic breadth of tempt is used by unbelief to allege a contradiction between Gen 22:1 and Jas 1:13, when the two texts use one English word for two entirely different acts.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a manufactured contradiction. Because the Authorized Version says God did tempt Abraham while James says God tempteth no man, the sceptic announces an error in Scripture and the careless believer is unsettled. The difficulty is entirely in the English. The Hebrew nasah and the Greek peirazo both mean to put to the test; whether that testing is holy or wicked depends on the intent of the one who applies it. A physician and a poisoner may both administer a substance; the act is not the same act. God proves His people to reveal and strengthen what He has given them; Satan probes them to find a place to break them. James is denying the second of God, not the first, and he says so in the next breath: every man is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust and enticed.

Recover the plain sense: God tests, and testing is a mercy. Gen 22 is not a trap laid for Abraham but the occasion on which his faith was brought into daylight and God provided a substitute on the mount — the whole scene preaching a better Father and a better Son. And guard the third sense most carefully, because it is the one modern religion commits without noticing. Demanding that God act on cue to settle a doubt, laying out conditions He must meet to prove His love, treating obedience as leverage — that is tempting God at Massah, and our Lord refused to do it even when the devil quoted Scripture to suggest it.
roots_summary: Latin tentare, to try — a neutral word for testing, whose morality lies in the tester’s purpose.
roots_lines: Tempt — Latin tentare, to handle, try, prove.
Hebrew nasah, to put to the proof (Gen 22:1; Deu 6:16).
Greek peirazo, to test — used of God’s proving and of Satan’s enticing alike.
God tests to refine; Satan tests to destroy; man tempts God by demanding proof.
Massah means testing — the place named for the sin committed there (Exo 17:7).
usage: Gen 22:1 and Jas 1:13 use one English word for two different acts — no contradiction.
Deu 6:16 defines the sin of Massah: requiring God to prove Himself on demand.
Mat 4:7 shows our Lord refusing a sign even when Scripture was quoted to urge it.

etymology: From the Latin declarare, to make clear — de, intensive, and clarus, clear. To make a thing plain and open which was hidden, obscure, or unknown. It renders the Hebrew nagad, to make conspicuous, and the Greek exegeomai, to lead out into view.
biblical_def: To declare is to make manifest, and Scripture assigns the work to four declarers. The creation declares: “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psa 19:1) — a testimony without speech, going out to the end of the world, which leaves every man without excuse. God Himself declares, and does so in a way no creature can imitate: “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand” (Isa 46:10). Prophecy is here made the proof of deity, and note the ground of it — He can announce the end because He has decreed it. A god who merely foresaw would be a spectator; the God of Isaiah declares the end because His counsel stands. Third, the Son declares the Father: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Joh 1:18). The Greek is exegesato — He has expounded Him, led Him out into view. Christ is not merely a messenger about God but the exegesis of God. And fourth, the resurrection declares the Son, “declared to be the Son of God with power” (Rom 1:4) — not made so, but publicly proclaimed to be what He eternally was.
webster_summary: To make clear, manifest, or known; to publish, to proclaim. In Scripture, the work of creation, of God, of the Son, and of the resurrection.
webster_full: DECLARE, v.t. To clear; to free from obscurity; to make plain.
To make known; to tell explicitly; to manifest or communicate.
To publish; to proclaim; to announce openly before witnesses.
From the Latin declarare, from de and clarus, clear.
In law, to state the plaintiff’s case; hence, a formal and public setting-forth.
scriptures: Psa 19:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork .
Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Joh 1:18
No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
Rom 1:4
And declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead:
corruption_summary: Rom 1:4 is regularly pressed by adoptionists to mean Christ was made the Son at the resurrection, when declared means openly proclaimed to be what He always was.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is adoptionism, ancient and recurring. Because Paul writes that Christ was declared to be the Son of God with power by the resurrection, it is argued that sonship began there — that Jesus was a man elevated to divine status at His vindication. The word forbids it. To declare is to make plain what is already the case; a verdict declares a man guilty, it does not make him so. The same Apostle in the same sentence has already called Him God’s Son, made of the seed of David according to the flesh, which presupposes a Son who existed to be so made. And Joh 1:18 settles it from the other side: the only begotten Son is in the bosom of the Father before He declares Him. Eternal generation is not a conclusion drawn from the empty tomb; the empty tomb is the public proclamation of it.

Recover the plain sense: the resurrection is God’s open verdict on His Son, reversing the judgment of the court that condemned Him. Men declared Him a blasphemer; God declared Him the Son of God with power. Hold this together with Psa 19:1 and Isa 46:10 and the doctrine of revelation stands complete. The heavens declare enough of God’s glory to leave men inexcusable, but not enough to save; prophecy declares that His counsel stands; and the Son declares the Father Himself, which no star and no prophet could do. What creation whispers and prophecy announces, Christ exegetes.
roots_summary: Latin de + clarus, to make clear — the making-manifest of what is hidden, culminating in the Son who expounds the Father.
roots_lines: Declare — Latin declarare, from clarus, clear.
Hebrew nagad, to make conspicuous, to set before the face (Psa 19:1).
Greek exegeomai, to lead out, expound — whence exegesis (Joh 1:18).
To declare is to publish what is, never to constitute what was not (Rom 1:4).
Isa 46:10 grounds predictive prophecy in the decree: My counsel shall stand.
usage: Joh 1:18: Christ is the exegesis of the Father, not merely a report about Him.
Rom 1:4 declares, and does not create, the eternal Sonship.
Isa 46:10 makes foretelling the proof of deity because the counsel is God’s own.

etymology: From the Saxon be, an intensive prefix, and maenan, to moan or lament. To moan over a person — the preposition is the point, for bemoaning is grief directed toward another, not merely felt within oneself.
biblical_def: To bemoan is to lament for someone, and Scripture treats the presence or absence of such lament as a measure of a people’s standing. Jeremiah’s question over the ruined city is unbearable precisely because it expects the answer none: “who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou doest?” (Jer 15:5). To be unmourned is the last stage of desolation; Nineveh receives the same sentence — “who will bemoan her?” (Nah 3:7). More solemn still is Jer 16:5, where the LORD forbids the prophet to lament at all: Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them. When God withdraws permission to grieve, judgment has passed beyond the reach of tears. And Jeremiah teaches the church how to aim its sorrow rightly: “Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away” (Jer 22:10). The dead are past our help; the man carried into exile who shall return no more is the fitter object of grief. That principle governs Christian mourning still. We sorrow for the departed saint, but not as others which have no hope; the heavier weeping belongs to those going away from God while still alive.
webster_summary: To lament or bewail on another’s behalf; to express grief for a person or place. To be unbemoaned is, in the prophets, the mark of a completed judgment.
webster_full: BEMOAN, v.t. To lament; to bewail; to express sorrow for.
From the Saxon be and maenan, to moan, to complain.
Distinguished from mere moaning by its object: one bemoans another, not oneself.
In the prophets, to be left unbemoaned is the extremity of desolation (Jer 15:5; Nah 3:7).
The prohibition of bemoaning is itself a judgment (Jer 16:5).
scriptures: Jer 15:5
For who shall have pity upon thee, O Jerusalem? or who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou doest?
Jer 16:5
For thus saith the LORD, Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them: for I have taken away my peace from this people, saith the LORD, even lovingkindness and mercies.
Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country.
Nah 3:7
And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?
corruption_summary: Modern religion has largely lost public lament, treating sustained grief as a problem to be resolved rather than a duty owed — while Scripture makes the absence of mourners a sign of judgment, not of health.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the abolition of lament. Contemporary church life has little room for sorrow that does not resolve within the hour; grief is handled as a stage to be moved through, and the mourner is quietly urged toward recovery so that the congregation may return to its accustomed brightness. Scripture is far more spacious. A third of the Psalter laments, an entire book is called Lamentations, and the prophets bemoan cities aloud and at length. Jeremiah did not weep because he lacked faith; he wept because he saw clearly. To lose the vocabulary of lament is not to become more joyful but to become shallower, and it leaves the genuinely bereaved with no language the church will accept.

Recover the plain sense: bemoaning is an act of love aimed outward, and Jer 22:10 tells us where to aim it hardest. We instinctively pour our grief upon the dead, where it can do nothing, and withhold it from the living who are walking away. Reverse that. Weep sore for the son who goeth away, for the friend hardening under the word, for the nation being carried off — those are the mourners’ proper business. And take Jer 16:5 as a warning: there is a point at which God forbids the tears, and it is a mercy to be still permitted to weep.
roots_summary: Saxon be + maenan, to moan over — grief directed toward another, whose absence marks a finished judgment.
roots_lines: Bemoan — Saxon intensive be + maenan, to moan, lament.
The prefix carries the sense over or for: to moan on another’s account.
Jer 15:5 and Nah 3:7: to be unbemoaned is the last stage of ruin.
Jer 16:5: God may forbid lament, and the prohibition is itself judgment.
Jer 22:10 orders the priority — weep more for the exile than for the dead.
usage: Jer 22:10 redirects grief from the dead, past help, to the living going away.
To be left with no one to bemoan you is the prophets’ picture of total desolation.
Jer 16:5 shows that permission to mourn is itself a mercy.

etymology: From the Saxon intensive be and wail, of Norse origin (vaela, to lament) — to wail over. Like bemoan, the prefix directs the grief toward an object outside the mourner.
biblical_def: Bewail is loud, visible grief, and Scripture both regulates it and requires it. It is regulated at the tabernacle door, where Aaron and his surviving sons are forbidden to mourn their own dead: “Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die” — but the congregation may bewail the burning which the LORD hath kindled (Lev 10:6). The priest in the middle of his ministry may not stop to weep for Nadab and Abihu, for he stands there in an office; the people may weep for him. Grief has an order, and office may override affection. It is permitted to the captive woman, who shall “bewail her father and her mother a full month” (Deu 21:13) before she is taken to wife — a striking humanity in the law of war, granting a foreign woman a full month of sorrow and forbidding her to be treated as spoil. It appears in Jephthah’s daughter, who asks to go and “bewail my virginity” (Jdg 11:37), and in the prophet who says, “I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer the vine of Sibmah” (Isa 16:9) — God’s own messenger weeping over a heathen land under judgment. And Paul turns the word upon the church: he fears he shall “bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented” (2Co 12:21). The apostle weeps not over the dead but over the unrepentant living.
webster_summary: To express deep sorrow for, aloud and openly; to lament over. Regulated in the law, permitted to the captive, and turned by the Apostle upon the impenitent.
webster_full: BEWAIL, v.t. To bemoan; to lament; to express sorrow for, with outward signs.
From be and wail; the wailing is audible and visible, not merely inward.
Applied to the dead, to a calamity, or to a condition, as virginity (Jdg 11:37).
In the law, restrained upon the officiating priest (Lev 10:6) and granted to the captive (Deu 21:13).
In the Epistles, directed toward the sin of the impenitent living (2Co 12:21).
scriptures: Lev 10:6

And Moses said unto Aaron, and unto Eleazar and unto Ithamar, his sons, Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die, and lest wrath come upon all the people: but let your brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning which the LORD hath kindled.

And she shall put the raiment of her captivity from off her, and shall remain in thine house, and bewail her father and her mother a full month: and after that thou shalt go in unto her, and be her husband, and she shall be thy wife.
Isa 16:9
Therefore I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer the vine of Sibmah: I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh: for the shouting for thy summer fruits and for thy harvest is fallen.

And lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed.
corruption_summary: The one thing the modern church will not bewail is sin — grief over calamity is permitted and encouraged, while Paul’s weeping over the unrepentant is thought harsh or judgmental.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is selective sorrow. Congregations weep readily over disaster, illness, and death, and rightly so; but let a man grieve openly over a professing believer living in unrepented sin and he is charged with a want of love. The Apostle knew no such rule. He tells the Corinthians plainly that he expects to bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented, and he sets that grief alongside his fear of being humbled by God among them. Note that Paul does not describe himself as angry with them, nor as writing them off. He describes himself as mourning — the posture of a man who loves people he cannot approve.

Recover the plain sense: godly sorrow over sin, one’s own and others’, is not censoriousness but the plainest evidence of love. The censorious man is gratified by another’s fall; the man who bewails it is wounded by it. Lev 10:6 adds the balancing truth that grief must sometimes yield to duty — Aaron stood in his office with his sons dead in the sanctuary, and was not permitted to leave the altar to mourn. There is a time to weep and a time to serve while weeping is forbidden, and only a mind shaped by Scripture can tell which hour it is.
roots_summary: Saxon be + Norse vaela, to wail over — open, audible grief, regulated by office and aimed at last upon sin.
roots_lines: Bewail — intensive be + wail (Norse vaela, to lament).
The mourning is outward: rent clothes, uncovered head, audible cry.
Lev 10:6 restrains the priest in office from bewailing his own dead.
Deu 21:13 grants the captive woman a full month to bewail her parents.
2Co 12:21 turns the word upon unrepented sin in the church.
usage: Lev 10:6: office may forbid a man to stop and mourn; the congregation mourns for him.
Deu 21:13 shows the law’s humanity toward a captive — a full month of grief.
2Co 12:21: Paul’s tears over the impenitent are love, not censoriousness.

etymology: From the Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify — the intensive prefix with fright. To strike with sudden and overpowering fear, stronger than to alarm and more sudden than to dread.
biblical_def: Affright is terror used as a weapon, and its chief biblical instance shows exactly how the enemy of God’s people fights. Sennacherib’s officers stood beneath the wall of Jerusalem and “cried with a loud voice in the Jews’ speech unto the people of Jerusalem that were on the wall, to affright them, and to trouble them; that they might take the city” (2Ch 32:18). Mark the strategy. They shouted in Hebrew, not Assyrian, so that the common people on the wall would understand and lose heart. The object was stated plainly: that they might take the city. Terror was the siege engine; the walls were to be brought down from the inside, by the fears of the men standing on them. That is still the method. The adversary speaks in a language the saints understand, aims at the defenders rather than the defences, and seeks to win by fear what he cannot win by force. Scripture’s answer is not that the danger is imaginary — Sennacherib was a real king with a real army — but that the LORD is greater: with him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles. The word appears elsewhere of men astonished at the ruin of the wicked (Job 18:20), where the terror is not a weapon but a warning.
webster_summary: To impress with sudden fear; to terrify. In Scripture, chiefly the enemy’s deliberate use of terror as a means of conquest.
webster_full: AFFRIGHT, v.t. To impress with sudden fear; to frighten; to terrify or alarm.
From the Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify; the prefix intensive.
Stronger than alarm, which may be momentary; affright overpowers.
Used of terror employed as a stratagem of war (2Ch 32:18).
In the passive, to be struck with astonishment at a judgment (Job 18:20).
scriptures: Then they cried with a loud voice in the Jews' speech unto the people of Jerusalem that were on the wall, to affright them, and to trouble them; that they might take the city.
They that come after him shall be astonied at his day, as they that went before were affrighted .
Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude that is with him: for there be more with us than with him:
With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles. And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
corruption_summary: Fear is now marketed continuously as a means of managing populations and selling remedies, which is precisely the Rabshakeh’s method — terror aimed at the defenders in a language they understand.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the industrial use of dread. Whole trades now depend upon keeping people affrighted: the endless cycle of alarm that sells news, the crisis that must never be allowed to pass, the appeal that opens by describing a catastrophe and closes by naming its price. The technique is old enough to be described in 2Ch 32. Speak in the people’s own tongue; address the ordinary men on the wall rather than the king in his palace; magnify the enemy; and above all suggest that their God cannot deliver them. Hezekiah’s answer is the model of a right response — he neither denied the Assyrian army nor conceded its conclusion, but set the arm of flesh against the LORD our God, and then went and spread the letter before the LORD.

Recover the plain sense: the Christian is not promised freedom from danger but is forbidden the paralysis that danger aims to produce. Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria was said while the king of Assyria was actually at the gate. Fear of God is the appointed cure for the fear of man, because a soul genuinely afraid of the Almighty has very little capacity left for being affrighted by anyone else. The Rabshakeh took no city that day. The angel of the LORD went out, and the great king went home with shame of face.
roots_summary: Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify — sudden overwhelming fear, used by the enemy as a siege weapon against the defenders’ hearts.
roots_lines: Affright — Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify; intensive of fright.
Stronger and more sudden than alarm or dread.
2Ch 32:18: terror deliberately employed that they might take the city.
The Rabshakeh spoke in the Jews’ speech so the common people would understand.
Job 18:20: men affrighted at the day of the wicked — terror as warning, not weapon.
usage: 2Ch 32:18 states the aim of terror outright: to take the city by the fears of its defenders.
Hezekiah answers not by denying the danger but by naming a greater help (2Ch 32:8).
The fear of God is the appointed antidote to the fear of man.

etymology: The older form of astonished, from the Old French estoner, to stun, and ultimately the Latin ex and tonare, to thunder — literally to be thunderstruck. The Authorized Version keeps astonied where the sense is stunned into silence and stillness, not merely surprised.
biblical_def: Astonied is stronger than astonished has since become: it is the condition of a man struck dumb and motionless, thunderstruck. Ezra hears of the mingled marriages and does not argue — “I rent my garment and my mantle, and plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat down astonied” (Ezr 9:3), and he sits so until the evening sacrifice, surrounded by everyone that trembled at the words of the God of Israel. That is what sin looks like when it is genuinely seen: not a discussion, but a man on the ground unable to speak. Job says upright men shall be astonied at the prosperity of the hypocrite (Job 17:8), the honest bewilderment of the godly at a world that appears to reward the false. And the word rises to its height in the fourth Servant Song: “As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man” (Isa 52:14). The crowd is thunderstruck at the Sufferer — not at His glory but at His disfigurement. The same chapter that promises He shall sprinkle many nations opens with men unable to look at Him. Both belong to the Servant: a face marred beyond recognition, and kings shutting their mouths before Him. The astonishment of Isa 52:14 is the necessary road to the astonishment of Isa 52:15.
webster_summary: Stunned; struck dumb with amazement, grief, or horror; the older and stronger form of astonished, implying silence and immobility.
webster_full: ASTONIED, pp. The old form of astonished; stunned; confounded with fear or wonder.
From the Old French estoner, to stun; Latin ex and tonare, to thunder.
Implying more than surprise: the loss of speech and motion (Ezr 9:3–4).
Applied to horror at a spectacle of suffering (Isa 52:14).
Applied to the perplexity of upright men at the prosperity of the wicked (Job 17:8).
scriptures: Ezr 9:3
And when I heard this thing, I rent my garment and my mantle, and plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat down astonied.
Job 17:8
Upright men shall be astonied at this, and the innocent shall stir up himself against the hypocrite.
As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men:
Dan 4:19

Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him. The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee. Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies.
corruption_summary: An age saturated with spectacle has lost the capacity to be astonied — and the first casualty is any real sense of sin, which Ezra met by sitting on the ground until the evening sacrifice.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is one of capacity rather than definition. Astonishment requires a settled sense of what ought to be, against which an outrage registers as an outrage; where nothing is expected, nothing can shock. A generation fed continuous spectacle and continuous scandal has been trained out of the reaction, so that atrocities scroll past between advertisements and the word shocking now means merely notable. The church has not escaped this. Sin reported among God’s people is discussed, managed, and moved past; almost no one sits down astonied.

Recover the plain sense: Ezra’s posture is instructive precisely because it is so extreme and so unhurried. He tore his garment, pulled out his hair, and sat until the evening sacrifice — hours of silence before he prayed a word. And when he prayed, he did not say they but we: our iniquities are increased over our head. That is what it looks like to be thunderstruck by sin rather than merely informed of it. Set beside it Isa 52:14, where men are astonied at the marred visage of the Servant, and the two astonishments meet: what sin is, and what it cost. A soul that has felt either will not be easily bored by the gospel.
roots_summary: Latin ex + tonare, to thunder — struck dumb and still; the older, stronger form of astonished.
roots_lines: Astonied — Old French estoner, to stun; Latin ex + tonare, to thunder.
The same root gives stun, astonish, and astound.
Implies silence and immobility, not mere surprise (Ezr 9:3).
Isa 52:14: men astonied at the marred visage of the Servant.
The AV retains the older form where the stunning is total.
usage: Ezr 9:3–4: the right reaction to discovered sin is silence before it is speech.
Isa 52:14 and 52:15 pair the two astonishments — at His marring and at His sprinkling.
Job 17:8: the upright are astonied at the prosperity of the hypocrite.

etymology: From the Old French compasser, to go round, measure with a compass — Latin com, together, and passus, a step. To surround, encircle, or go about a thing; in the Authorized Version always with the idea of a complete ring closed about an object.
biblical_def: Compassed describes a ring closed about someone, and Scripture uses it for both the encirclements that destroy and the encirclements that save. It is the ring of enemies: the men of Sodom “compassed the house round, both old and young” (Gen 19:4), a whole city with no righteous remnant; and our Lord’s warning, “when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh” (Luk 21:20). It is the ring of affliction, in the mouth of a man sinking: “the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me” (Jon 2:3) — and Jonah is careful to say thy billows, for he knows whose hand is in the sea. It is the ring of obedience at Jericho, where “the ark of the LORD compassed the city” (Josh 6:11) day after day with no visible effect, until the seventh day brought down what no ram had touched. And it is the ring of witnesses: “seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight” (Heb 12:1). The picture is not of spectators watching from the stands but of those who have already run, encircling the course as testimony that the race can be finished. The Christian is surrounded either way; the question is by what.
webster_summary: Encircled; surrounded on every side; gone round about. Used of besieging enemies, of overwhelming affliction, of ritual procession, and of the witnesses encircling the believer’s race.
webster_full: COMPASS, v.t. To stretch round; to encircle; to environ; to surround.
To go or walk round: they compassed the city seven times (Josh 6:15).
To besiege; to invest with armed force (Luk 21:20).
From the Old French compasser; Latin com and passus, a step.
Figuratively, to be enclosed by circumstances, as with sorrows or with witnesses (Jon 2:3; Heb 12:1).
scriptures: Gen 19:4
But before they lay down, the men of the city, even the men of Sodom, compassed the house round, both old and young, all the people from every quarter:
Josh 6:11
So the ark of the LORD compassed the city, going about it once : and they came into the camp, and lodged in the camp.
Jon 2:3
For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me.
Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
corruption_summary: Heb 12:1 is habitually preached as though the cloud of witnesses were a heavenly audience watching us perform, which turns a word of encouragement into a source of self-consciousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is turning witnesses into spectators. The popular image has the saints of Hebrews 11 seated in a stadium observing the believer’s progress, cheering or wincing as he runs — a picture which, however well meant, puts the runner on stage and makes his race a performance before an audience of the perfected. The Greek word is martyres, those who bear testimony. The eleventh chapter has just paraded them precisely as men and women who testified by faith: Abel testifying though dead, Noah condemning the world, Abraham looking for a city, Moses esteeming reproach greater riches. They do not watch us run; they surround the track as evidence that the course is passable and the promises are worth it.

Recover the plain sense: the encouragement is evidential, not theatrical. You are hemmed in by a great crowd of proofs. And notice how Heb 12:1 uses the encirclement — therefore lay aside every weight, and run looking unto Jesus. The eyes go forward to the Author and Finisher, not sideways to the crowd. Set this beside the other rings and the comfort deepens: Sodom compassed Lot’s house and angels struck it blind; the floods compassed Jonah and God spoke to the fish; armies compassed Jerusalem in judgment; and Israel compassed Jericho in obedience until the walls fell flat. To be surrounded is not the same as to be lost.
roots_summary: Latin com + passus, to step around — a closed ring, whether of enemies, of floods, of ritual obedience, or of testifying saints.
roots_lines: Compassed — Old French compasser, to go round; Latin com + passus, a step.
The same root gives the mariner’s compass and the draughtsman’s compasses.
Of siege: Jerusalem compassed with armies (Luk 21:20).
Of ritual: the ark compassed Jericho once daily, seven times on the seventh (Josh 6:11).
Heb 12:1 martyres — witnesses who testify, not spectators who watch.
usage: Heb 12:1: the cloud surrounds as evidence, not as an audience; the eyes go to Christ.
Jon 2:3 says thy billows — the drowning man names whose hand is in the sea.
Josh 6:11: obedience that showed no result for six days brought the wall down on the seventh.

etymology: From the Old French buffe, a blow, whence buffet, a cuff or slap with the fist or open hand. It renders the Greek kolaphizo, to strike with the knuckles — not the formal stroke of a scourge but the contemptuous blow of a man’s hand.
biblical_def: To buffet is to be struck with the fist, and the word carries a peculiar sting because such a blow is not punishment but insult. It belongs first to the Passion. “Some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to buffet him, and to say unto him, Prophesy” (Mar 14:65); “Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him” (Mat 26:67). They blindfolded Him first, so that the game was to strike and demand He name the striker — the Son of God, whose eyes are as a flame of fire, mocked as a blind man who cannot tell who hit Him. From that scene the word passes to His servants. Paul lists it among the marks of apostleship: “we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace” (1Co 4:11). And it is the word he chooses for his thorn: “there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me” (2Co 12:7). Observe the theology packed into that verse — the thorn is given (a divine passive), it is Satan’s messenger, and its purpose is to keep an apostle from being exalted above measure. The devil strikes; God aims the blow. Peter completes the doctrine: there is no glory in being buffeted for your faults, but to suffer for well-doing and take it patiently “this is acceptable with God” (1Pe 2:20).
webster_summary: To strike with the hand or fist; a blow of contempt rather than of formal punishment. Suffered by Christ in the Passion and by His servants after Him.
webster_full: BUFFET, n. A blow with the fist or open hand; a cuff; a slap.
BUFFET, v.t. To strike with the hand; to box; to beat.
From the Old French buffe, a blow; of imitative origin.
Rendering the Greek kolaphizo, to strike with the knuckles (Mat 26:67; 2Co 12:7).
Figuratively, to contend against, as to buffet the waves.
scriptures: Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him; and others smote him with the palms of their hands,
And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to buffet him, and to say unto him, Prophesy: and the servants did strike him with the palms of their hands.

And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure.
For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.
corruption_summary: 2Co 12:7 is regularly preached as though the thorn were merely an inconvenience to be claimed and removed, when Paul names it Satan’s messenger, given by God, and left in place by a refusal three times repeated.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the promise of guaranteed relief. Whole ministries teach that persistent affliction in a believer indicates a deficiency — too little faith, unconfessed sin, a prayer not prayed with sufficient authority — and that the thorn may always be extracted by the right technique. Paul’s account destroys the doctrine at every point. He was an apostle, caught up to the third heaven, and he besought the Lord thrice; and the answer was not removal but My grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness. The buffeting continued. If unrelieved affliction proved a defect of faith, the chief of the apostles stands convicted by his own epistle.

Recover the plain sense: the passive there was given is the hinge of the verse. Satan supplies the messenger, but the giving is God’s, and the stated purpose is God’s — lest I should be exalted above measure. Here is the whole doctrine of providence in one sentence: the enemy’s malice is real, and it is nevertheless an instrument in a Father’s hand, aimed at a mercy the apostle could not have obtained any other way. Set 1Pe 2:20 beside it and the believer’s duty is plain. Buffeting deserved is no credit to anyone; buffeting endured patiently for well-doing is acceptable with God — and the Master was buffeted first, blindfolded, and told to prophesy.
roots_summary: Old French buffe, a blow — the contemptuous strike of a fist; borne by Christ, then by His servants, and aimed by God even when dealt by Satan.
roots_lines: Buffet — Old French buffe, a blow with the hand.
Greek kolaphizo, to strike with the knuckles (Mat 26:67).
A blow of insult rather than of judicial punishment.
2Co 12:7: the thorn is given — a divine passive over a satanic messenger.
1Pe 2:20 distinguishes buffeting for faults from buffeting for well-doing.
usage: Mar 14:65: they blindfolded Him first, making the blow a game — insult, not sentence.
2Co 12:7 holds Satan’s malice and God’s purpose in a single sentence.
1Pe 2:20: only suffering for well-doing, patiently borne, is acceptable with God.
